newsitem.title: USA: Centerior, Ohio Edison reaction mixed.
newsitem.headline: Centerior, Ohio Edison reaction mixed.

text.p: A proposed merger between Ohio Edison Co and Centerior Energy Corp drew a mixed reaction from analysts, with some questioning whether Ohio Edison would benefit from joining forces with a weaker electric utility.

"I'm not sure if it's positive for Ohio Edison because I think Ohio Edison takes on more financial risk by joining up with a weaker company," said Barry Abramson of Prudential Securities Research. "I'm not sure that the very, very long-term savings are positive enough to offset...the higher risk."
Ohio Edison was off 1-1/8 to 19-3/4 Monday, while Centerior rose 1-5/8 to 9-1/4 after the companies announced a definitive agreement to merge in a tax-free stock transaction.
The companies said they expect to save $1 billion over 10 years and to pay down debt faster than either company could individually.
"We think it's good for the Centerior Energy holder and obviously questionable for the Ohio Edison holder," said Andrew Levi of Furman Selz.
He said Ohio Edison may seek more control over nuclear plants that Centerior now operates.

Several years ago, Ohio Edison and Centerior, along with DQE Inc's Duquesne Light Co. in Pennsylvania, formed a venture called Central Area Power Coordination Group to build and operate power generating plants, including four nuclear plants in Ohio and Pennsylvania.

If the merger is completed, the combined company -- to be called FirstEnergy Corp -- will have at least a majority stake in each of the group's nine coal and nuclear generating units and will have operational control of seven of the nine.
Centerior now operates two of the nuclear plants and Duquesne the other two.

"Although (Ohio Edison has) no real experience operating nuclear plants, (its) management...is much better respected within the Wall Street community than the Centerior management was," Levi said. Centerior has been improving its nuclear operations, he added.
Levi said Centerior has set discounted rates with many industrial customers, which will mean some revenue erosion.
He rates shares in both companies at hold.
"The plan as it is presented would basically give you a stock price for Ohio Edison, we think, about where it is right now -- about $20-$21," Levi said.
Abramson previously rated Ohio Edison at hold and Centerior at sell, and he said the merger announcement had not changed his view.
At least one analyst views the proposal a "win-win" deal for both companies -- McDonald & Co's Nancy Benacci.
Noting McDonald provided the fairness opinion, she said the companies expect the merger to be accretive for earnings and cash flow in the first year after its completion, expected by January 1, 1998.
She cited Ohio Edison's track record in cutting costs. She also said faster debt reduction and the new entity's greater control over the power generating units should prove beneficial.
"(The merger) really provides them with the right kind of combination to exist profitably in a deregulated environment," she said.
